page6_img_1.png.title: Windows Vista data‑collection timeline
page6_img_1.png.description: A horizontal timeline showing when development metrics and failures were gathered for Windows Vista. The left tick is labeled “Windows Server 2003 – SP1” and the right tick is the “Vista Release”; a dashed arrow between them (labeled “Collect product metrics (commits, code churn, complexity, etc.)”) indicates that pre-release product/development metrics were collected from the earlier milestone up to the release. To the right of the Vista Release an arrow is labeled “6 months to collect failures,” indicating post-release failures were gathered for six months after shipping. The x‑axis is labeled “Time.”

page3_img_1.png.title: Contribution network showing component A linked via developers Fred and Ram
page3_img_1.png.description: Diagram of a contribution (bipartite) network: circles are software components and rounded rectangles are developers. The central blue circle labeled A is connected by dashed contribution edges to two developer nodes, Fred (left) and Ram (right); Fred is also connected to components D and E (above and below him) and Ram is also connected to components F and G. This topology illustrates shared authorship — A is indirectly related to D, E, F and G through its contributors, highlighting the latent socio-technical links the paper uses to explain why a component with few direct dependencies may still be important or failure-prone.

page9_img_1.png.title: ROC curves comparing predictive models across Eclipse releases 3.0–3.3
page9_img_1.png.description: Four side-by-side ROC plots (releases 3.0, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3) show True Positive Rate vs False Positive Rate for four logistic models trained on the prior release: Socio-Technical (blue solid), Combined (green dashed), Dependency (black dotted), and Contribution (red dot-dash). Across the panels the blue socio-technical curve generally lies above the others (higher true positive rates for the same false positive rate), with the green combined curve close behind, while the dependency and contribution models consistently underperform. Release-specific detail: in release 3.2 the combined model briefly matches or slightly exceeds the socio-technical model at very low false-positive rates, but by release 3.3 the socio-technical model shows the clearest separation and best discrimination. Overall the figure visually supports the paper’s claim that socio-technical and combined network measures produce higher AUCs and better fault-prioritization than dependency- or contribution-only models.

page3_img_2.png.title: Dependency network: A depends on B and C; B depends on C
page3_img_2.png.description: A small directed dependency graph of three software components labeled A, B and C (Figure 1b). Solid arrows represent directed dependency relations: A has outgoing edges to B and to C (A depends on B and C), and B has an outgoing edge to C (B depends on C). The diagram (A shaded blue, B and C shaded green) matches the paper’s running example where A has two dependencies and no dependents, illustrating a case where dependency structure alone may understate A’s importance without considering other relation types.

page7_img_1.png.title: Eclipse release timeline with development and defect data windows
page7_img_1.png.description: A horizontal timeline showing Eclipse release milestones (1.0 Nov 2001, 2.0 June 2002, 2.1 March 2003, 3.0 June 2004) and the intervals used for data collection. Bidirectional arrows mark the development-data window for each release (e.g., "2.0 Dev Data" spans from 1.0 to 2.0; "2.1 Dev Data" spans from 2.0 to 2.1; "3.0 Dev Data" spans from 2.1 to 3.0) and the defect-data window following each release (e.g., "2.0 Defect Data" spans 2.0 to 2.1; "2.1 Defect Data" spans 2.1 to 3.0). The figure illustrates the paper’s procedure: for release R_i development activity is taken from the interval [R_{i-1}, R_i] and post-release defects are measured in [R_i, R_{i+1}], with further releases indicated to the right.

page3_img_3.png.title: Socio-technical network: component A linked via developers to highly connected binaries
page3_img_3.png.description: Combined socio-technical graph (circles = software components A–G; rectangles = developers Fred and Ram) that overlays dependency edges (solid, directed arrows) and contribution edges (dashed, undirected lines). The central blue node A is shown connected to both Fred and Ram by dashed contribution links; those two developers in turn connect to other binaries (D and E on Fred’s side, F and G on Ram’s) that have many dependency arrows indicating high connectivity in the dependency subgraph. A also has directed dependency links to B and C, so in the aggregated view A gains indirect ties to influential components via shared authorship—illustrating the latent socio-technical paths that can reveal a component’s importance (and thus help explain why A might be failure-prone) even when dependency-only or contribution-only graphs do not highlight it.

page8_img_2.png.title: Cross-release prediction performance (AUC, Precision, Recall, F‑Score, Nagelkerke) for Eclipse releases
page8_img_2.png.description: Table of prediction results when models trained on release r−1 are used to predict failure‑prone plugins in release r (rows for releases 2.1, 3.0–3.3). For each release the table reports five evaluation metrics (AUC, Precision, Recall, F‑Score, Nagelkerke) for four network-based models: Dependency, Contribution, Combined, and Socio‑technical. Overall the socio‑technical model most often achieves the highest AUC and F‑Score (for example, release 3.3: AUC=0.927, Precision=0.827, Recall=0.847, F‑Score=0.837), while the Combined model attains the highest AUC and precision in some releases (e.g., release 3.2: AUC=0.910, Precision=0.900). Shaded/bold cells mark the best-performing model per metric and release, illustrating that either the Combined or Socio‑technical models consistently outperform the Dependency and Contribution models across these cross‑release predictions.

page8_img_1.png.title: Comparison of prediction metrics for Dependency/Contribution/Combined/Socio-technical models
page8_img_1.png.description: The table reports mean precision, recall, F-score and Nagelkerke R2 for logistic regression fault-prediction models built from four network types (Dependency, Contribution, Combined, Socio-technical) for Windows Vista and Eclipse releases 2.0–3.3, averaged over 50 random two‑thirds/one‑third splits. Cells shaded/bold indicate values that are statistically higher than both the dependency and contribution baselines. In Vista the Combined model attains precision 0.787, recall 0.681 and F‑score 0.730, while the Socio‑technical model has slightly higher recall and F‑score (0.705 and 0.736) and the largest Nagelkerke (0.520). Across Eclipse releases the Combined and Socio‑technical models generally dominate; for example Eclipse 3.2 shows Combined = precision 0.835, recall 0.866, F‑score 0.846, Nagelkerke 0.816, and Eclipse 3.3 shows Socio‑technical = 0.820/0.831/0.823/0.727, illustrating improved predictive performance when dependency and contribution information are combined.
